title: Job Market Paper
text:
Accountability on Political Terms
Why does extensive anti-corruption activity produce limited accountability for political elites? This project examines how political and institutional contexts shape the outcomes of corruption prosecutions in Nigeria. Drawing on original case data and qualitative evidence, I investigate the challenges of holding powerful political actors legally accountable.

title: Working Papers
text:
Working Papers

1. Who Gets Convicted? The Political Economy of Corruption Prosecution Outcomes in Nigeria
With Muhammed Alakitan
This project examines why corruption and financial crime prosecutions in Nigeria produce different outcomes across defendants. Using a dataset of more than 6,000 trials, we assess how the relative balance of power between prosecutors and defendants shapes the likelihood and speed of conviction or acquittal.



2. The Politicization of Corruption Investigations in Comparative Perspective
This project examines how electoral politics shapes anti-corruption enforcement across countries. Using cross-national event data, the paper examines patterns in reported corruption investigations involving political elites.



3. Anti-Corruption Politicization in Nigeria
Why do some corruption allegations against politicians lead to prosecution while others do not? This project examines the progression from allegations and investigations to formal prosecution in Nigeria. Using an original dataset of cases involving political elites, it assesses how political relationships and institutional contexts shape which allegations reach the courts.



4. Why Do Some Pro-Government Militias Remobilize as Rebels? Ethnic Social Foundations and Militia Blowback
With Olusegun Somide | Under review
This paper examines why some pro-government militias become rebel groups after their relationship with the state ends. We combined statistical analysis with systematic within-case process tracing to investigate how militias’ social foundations shape their capacity to remobilize as armed opposition.

title: Teaching
text:
My teaching experience at Tulane University includes leading undergraduate discussion sections, supporting graduate quantitative methods class, delivering guest lectures, and facilitating R workshops. In methods instruction, I help students build confidence in research design and data analysis.


All appointments below are in the Department of Political Science at Tulane University and include leading weekly discussion sections and grading.



Fall 2026: Prof. Andrew Leber
Spring 2024: Prof. Moisés Arce

I support students in understanding political institutions, regime types, democratization, and contentious politics. Through discussion sections and feedback on assignments, I help students compare political systems and apply course concepts to contemporary events.





Spring 2025: Prof. Virginia Oliveros
Fall 2023: Prof. Stan Oklobdzija

I help undergraduate students develop foundational skills in political science research, including formulating research questions, evaluating evidence, measurement, and causal inference. My responsibilities include leading discussion sections, holding office hours, and providing feedback on research proposals and empirical assignments.





Fall 2024: Prof. Stan Oklobdzija

I supported graduate students in statistical analysis and applied research using R. The course covered regression models and approaches to causal inference, including regression discontinuity and difference-in-differences. I helped students work through problem sets, interpret statistical results, and apply quantitative methods to substantive research questions.






Introduction to Comparative Politics | November 4, 2026
Invited by Prof. Andrew Leber, Tulane University
I delivered a guest lecture on why ethnic identities become politically salient and how they shape cooperation and conflict. The session introduced essentialist, instrumentalist, constructivist, and institutionalist explanations of ethnic politics. Using examples from Kenya, Nigeria, Malawi, and Zambia, I guided students through how historical processes, political incentives, institutions, and group size shape ethnic mobilization.




Introduction to Comparative Politics | Spring 2024
Invited by Prof. Moisés Arce, Tulane University
I delivered a guest lecture examining how political institutions and ethnic cleavages shape conflict dynamics and fiscal policy. The session connected comparative political economy theories to empirical examples from Africa, Latin America, and other regions.




Scope and Methods | Fall 2023
Invited by Prof. Stan Oklobdzija, Tulane University
I delivered a guest lecture on informed consent, confidentiality, power dynamics in fieldwork, and the responsible use of administrative and survey data. The session explored practical ethical dilemmas in social science research, particularly research involving vulnerable populations.

title: Peer-Reviewed Publications
text:
Peer-Reviewed Publications

Where are the ethics? AI and the digital economy in Nigeria
Policy & Internet (2025), with M. Alakitan
This article investigates the ethical and governance challenges that accompany the rapid expansion of digital technologies and AI systems in Nigeria. We identify gaps in regulatory oversight and data protection that expose citizens to privacy violations and other digital harms. The paper argues for a stronger ethical and policy framework to guide responsible AI adoption in Nigeria’s public and private sectors.
Read Article



International political contexts, digital technologies, and political outcomes in Nigeria’s #EndSARS movement
Protest (2024), 4(1), 5–29
When do social movements achieve political outcomes? Existing research points to two key explanations: movements’ organizational infrastructure and the political opportunities structure. Focusing on the 2020 #EndSARS protest in Nigeria, I build on this literature to understand how and why social movements may achieve policy outcomes when social movements’ infrastructure and domestic political opportunities are relatively absent.
